name: Bronchiectasis Exacerbation

possible: Non-tuberculous mycobacteria (in chronic, treatment-refractory cases — separate workup)
pathogens.why: Bronchiectasis exacerbations are strongly influenced by individual chronic colonization patterns — Pseudomonas aeruginosa is disproportionately represented compared to typical community-acquired respiratory infections, particularly in patients with more severe or long-standing structural lung disease.

investigations.why: Tracks colonization status over time and directly informs both current and future empiric choices.

investigations.test: Chest X-ray (if new symptoms or to exclude complications)
investigations.why: Excludes pneumonia or other acute complications superimposed on chronic bronchiectatic changes.
Assesses for hypoxia, particularly relevant in patients with significant structural lung disease.

reason: A known bronchiectasis patient with increased sputum volume/purulence

meets criteria for an infective exacerbation. Antibiotic choice should be guided by prior sputum culture history where available, since bronchiectasis patients frequently have chronic colonization with specific organisms (notably Pseudomonas) that recur with each exacerbation.

clinicalPearls: Bronchiectasis is irreversible airway dilation, classically categorised as cylindrical/tubular (most common), varicose, or cystic; it may be focal or diffuse (Harrison 22e p.2242).

An acute exacerbation is defined primarily by a change in sputum character - increased volume and increased purulence - rather than by classic infection signs; fever and new infiltrates may be absent (Harrison 22e p.2243).
The usual clinical picture between exacerbations is a persistent productive cough with thick, tenacious sputum, often with crackles, wheeze, and sometimes digital clubbing (Harrison 22e p.2243).
Pseudomonas aeruginosa preferentially colonises damaged airways and evades host defences; its colonisation marks more severe disease and worse outcomes (Harrison 22e p.2242-2243, p.2244).

The pattern of lung-field involvement on imaging hints at the underlying cause: upper-zone in CF and post-radiation fibrosis, lower-zone in chronic aspiration/end-stage fibrosis/immunodeficiency, midlung in NTM (MAC) and dyskinetic cilia syndrome, and central-airway in ABPA (Harrison 22e p.2242-2243).
MAC-related bronchiectasis classically affects nonsmoking women over 50 years of age (Harrison 22e p.2242).
Up to 25-50% of patients referred for bronchiectasis have idiopathic disease after workup (Harrison 22e p.2242).
harrison.pathophysiology: The dominant mechanism of infectious bronchiectasis is the 'vicious cycle hypothesis': susceptibility to infection plus impaired mucociliary clearance permits microbial colonisation of the bronchial tree; the persistent microbial presence incites chronic inflammation that damages the airway wall, which further impairs secretion and microbial clearance, perpetuating the infectious-inflammatory cycle. Some organisms, notably Pseudomonas aeruginosa, are especially adept at colonising damaged airways and evading host defences. Impaired mucociliary clearance may be inherited (e.g., cystic fibrosis, dyskinetic cilia syndrome), and a single severe infection such as Bordetella pertussis or Mycoplasma pneumoniae can cause enough airway damage to seed the cycle. Pathologically there is small-airway wall inflammation with larger-airway wall destruction and dilation, and loss of elastin, smooth muscle, and cartilage; inflammatory cells release proteases, reactive oxygen species, and proinflammatory cytokines that damage larger airways while ongoing small-airway inflammation produces airflow obstruction. Antiproteases such as alpha-1 antitrypsin help neutralise neutrophil elastase, and bronchiectasis/emphysema occur in alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Molecular endotypes with distinct inflammatory and microbiome signatures may correlate with exacerbation risk. Noninfectious mechanisms include immune-mediated bronchial wall damage (e.g., Sjogren's syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis) and traction from parenchymal fibrosis. (Harrison 22e p.2242-2243)
additionalDifferentials: COPD - airflow obstruction on pulmonary function testing overlaps with bronchiectasis at presentation (Harrison 22e p.2243)
Asthma - may coexist; ABPA should be considered in refractory asthma (Harrison 22e p.2242-2243)
Cystic fibrosis - should be excluded early in any diffuse bronchiectasis workup (Harrison 22e p.2243)
infectionMimics: Nontuberculous mycobacterial (especially MAC) airway infection - organisms may be colonisers rather than true pathogens, complicating interpretation of positive cultures (Harrison 22e p.2243)
Active or reactivated tuberculosis (in endemic areas, a cause and mimic of recurrent airway infection) (Harrison 22e p.2242)
nonInfectiousMimics: Traction bronchiectasis from underlying lung fibrosis (e.g., idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, post-radiation fibrosis) - dilated airways from parenchymal distortion rather than active infection (Harrison 22e p.2242-2243)
Autoimmune/rheumatologic airway disease (rheumatoid arthritis, Sjogren's syndrome, inflammatory bowel disease) (Harrison 22e p.2242)
Recurrent aspiration (e.g., from esophageal motility disorders such as scleroderma) (Harrison 22e p.2242)
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution chest CT - imaging modality of choice; more specific than chest radiograph; look for airway dilation as 'tram tracks' or the 'signet-ring sign' (airway diameter at least 1.5x the adjacent vessel), lack of bronchial tapering, bronchial wall thickening, and inspissated secretions in a 'tree-in-bud' pattern (Harrison 22e p.2243)

Bronchoscopy - almost always required in focal bronchiectasis to exclude airway obstruction by mass or foreign body; consider with BAL in diffuse disease if no pathogen is identified (Harrison 22e p.2243)
Pulmonary function testing - functional assessment, typically showing mild-to-moderate airflow obstruction (Harrison 22e p.2243)

Etiologic workup for diffuse disease: sputum stains/cultures for bacteria, acid-fast bacilli, and fungi; immunoglobulin levels and CBC with differential; HIV testing; sweat chloride and genetic testing for CF; alpha-1 antitrypsin level; nasal/respiratory brush or biopsy for ciliary dyskinesia; autoimmune serologies; ABPA workup (Aspergillus skin test/precipitins, serum IgE, eosinophils); swallowing/neuromuscular assessment (Harrison 22e p.2242)
redFlags: Hemoptysis - bronchiectatic airways are dilated, inflamed, and highly vascular (supplied by the high-pressure bronchial circulation), so exacerbations can produce massive, life-threatening hemoptysis (Harrison 22e p.2243-2244, p.1408 hemoptysis chapter)
Massive hemoptysis - may require intubation to stabilise the patient, protection of the nonbleeding lung, and bronchial artery embolisation or surgery (Harrison 22e p.2244)
Emergence of antibiotic-resistant organisms after recurrent infections and repeated antibiotic courses (Harrison 22e p.2244)
harrison.prognosis: Outcomes vary widely with the underlying etiology and comorbidities, and are influenced by exacerbation frequency and, in infectious disease, the specific pathogens involved - Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonisation is associated with worse outcomes. Lung-function decline in non-CF bronchiectasis can resemble that of COPD, with FEV1 falling roughly 50-55 mL/year versus 20-30 mL/year in healthy controls. (Harrison 22e p.2244)
pitfalls: Expecting classic infection signs: an exacerbation may lack fever or new infiltrates, so reliance on these can miss it - the defining change is sputum volume and purulence (Harrison 22e p.2243).
Chest radiographs lack sensitivity for bronchiectasis; a normal or unremarkable film does not exclude it, and CT is needed for confirmation (Harrison 22e p.2243).

Positive NTM cultures may reflect colonisation rather than true infection; consensus diagnostic criteria (e.g., two positive sputum cultures, or one positive BAL, plus symptoms and radiographic findings) should be applied before attributing disease (Harrison 22e p.2243).
Focal bronchiectasis should prompt bronchoscopy to exclude an obstructing mass or foreign body rather than being attributed to infection alone (Harrison 22e p.2243).
